children.text: T3: Fabry–Pérot interferometer

Two identical parallel planar mirrors are separated by \(L\), with air inside and outside. They are symmetric under illumination from either side, lossless and partially reflecting. At normal incidence the reflected intensity is \(R\) times the incident intensity, where \(0<R<1\) and \(1-R\ll1\). A monochromatic laser of power \(P\) enters normally. The spacing is chosen so that no beam is reflected back and all incident power is transmitted.

nodes.alt: Original Fabry-Perot apparatus: laser of power P at left, two partially reflecting parallel mirrors separated by L and transmitted power P at right.

children.text: a
Show that the beam must acquire a nonzero phase shift \(\phi\) on passing through either mirror.
b
Find \(|\phi|\).
c
The incident beam is switched off rapidly. Find the total energy of light returning towards the laser after switch-off.
d
Estimate the duration of that returning pulse.

Phase convention: the official solution defines phi as the relative phase between a mirror's transmitted and reflected amplitudes. Use that convention here. An absolute transmission phase relative to the incident wave is not fixed by the supplied reflectivity alone.

statement.text:
T3: Fabry–Pérot interferometer
Two identical parallel planar mirrors are separated by \(L\), with air inside and outside. They are symmetric under illumination from either side, lossless and partially reflecting. At normal incidence the reflected intensity is \(R\) times the incident intensity, where \(0<R<1\) and \(1-R\ll1\). A monochromatic laser of power \(P\) enters normally. The spacing is chosen so that no beam is reflected back and all incident power is transmitted.

a
Show that the beam must acquire a nonzero phase shift \(\phi\) on passing through either mirror.
b
Find \(|\phi|\).
c
The incident beam is switched off rapidly. Find the total energy of light returning towards the laser after switch-off.
d
Estimate the duration of that returning pulse.
Phase convention: the official solution defines phi as the relative phase between a mirror's transmitted and reflected amplitudes. Use that convention here. An absolute transmission phase relative to the incident wave is not fixed by the supplied reflectivity alone.

children.text: T3: Fabry–Pérot interferometer
a and b. Complex amplitudes

Let \(r\) and \(t\) be amplitude reflection and transmission coefficients, with \(|r|^2=R\), \(|t|^2=1-R\). Write \(A\) for the incoming amplitude, \(B,C\) for the forward and backward intracavity waves at the first mirror, and \(D\) for the outgoing amplitude. Boundary conditions are
\[B=tA+rC,\qquad 0=rA+tC,\qquad D=tB,\qquad C=rBe^{2ikL}.\]

Eliminating amplitudes gives \(e^{-2ikL}=r^2-t^2\), hence \(|r^2-t^2|=1\). Losslessness gives \(|r|^2+|t|^2=1\). Equality in the complex triangle inequality requires \(r^2\) and \(-t^2\) to have the same phase. Thus
\[\operatorname{Re}(rt^*)=0,\qquad \phi=\arg t-\arg r=\pm\frac\pi2\pmod\pi,\qquad |\phi|=\frac\pi2.\]

This is the reflected-transmitted relative phase, as defined explicitly in the official solution. A common phase on both coefficients is not determined. The statement's wording about transmission alone needs this qualification. Some intermediate conjugate algebra in the source has incorrect signs, but its phase result follows from the triangle argument above.
Alternative: sum the reflected paths
\[A_\mathrm{back}=rA\left[1+\frac{t^2e^{2ikL}}{1-r^2e^{2ikL}}\right]=0.\]
The direct reflection and all multiply reflected transmitted paths form a geometric series. Its zero gives the same resonance equation and relative phase.
c. Stored energy and returning pulse

The initial forward intracavity power is \(P/(1-R)\), and the backward power is \(RP/(1-R)\). The stored energy is \(U=(1+R)LP/[c(1-R)]\), approximately \(2LP/[c(1-R)]\). At high reflectivity the release is almost symmetric, so the returning energy is approximately half of \(U\):
\[E_\mathrm{back}\simeq\frac{LP}{c(1-R)}.\]

The exact ideal abrupt-switch calculation clarifies the approximation. Once the incident wave disappears at the first mirror, the returning amplitude begins at \(-rA\). It is multiplied by \(r^2e^{2ikL}\) every round trip \(\Delta=2L/c\), so the returning powers are \(PR,PR^3,PR^5,\ldots\). Summing their energies gives
\[E_\mathrm{back}=\frac{2LPR}{c(1-R^2)}\simeq\frac{LP}{c(1-R)}.\]

The printed source series skips a power in one term. The exact geometric series above uses successive odd powers of the intensity reflectivity. The answer field requests the leading high-reflectivity result stated in the problem.
d. Pulse duration
The energy envelope decays as \(R^{2t/\Delta}\). Its time constant is
\[\tau_E=\frac{L}{c\ln(1/R)}\simeq\frac{L}{c(1-R)}.\]

The same estimate follows from \(-\dot U\simeq2P\), the energy escaping through both mirrors. Pulse duration is an estimate, and amplitude-decay time differs by a factor of two from the energy-decay time. The field explicitly checks the leading energy-envelope time constant, while other stated duration conventions require self-review.
Additional source approaches

nodes.alt: Original complex-plane triangle for a thin-mirror continuity argument, showing coefficients minus r, t and one, with a right angle between reflected and transmitted amplitudes.

children.text: If one additionally models each mirror as an ideal sheet with continuous electric field, \(1+r=t\). Together with losslessness, the complex coefficient triangle again makes \(r\) and \(t\) perpendicular. This continuity model is an extra assumption, not needed for the general result.

nodes.alt: Original one-sided illumination diagram: incoming amplitude A, reflected amplitude A sqrt(R) with phase theta, and transmitted amplitude A sqrt(1-R) with phase psi.
Original opposite-side illumination with amplitude and phase chosen so that its transmitted wave cancels the first diagram's leftward reflection.
Original superposition of both illumination cases: leftward waves cancel at the first mirror, with the two rightward outgoing waves and their phases shown.

children.text: A real-amplitude energy argument superposes those two illumination cases so the leftward outputs cancel. Equal total incoming and outgoing power requires \(\cos[2(\theta-\psi)]=-1\), hence the same quarter-cycle phase. The source's corresponding cosine equation has a typo. Its full original derivations and marking tables remain in the reference PDF.
